strengths: The paper addresses an identifiable research audience in Bayesian optimization and pure exploration: learning an approximately correct Pareto set over a continuous design space while controlling expensive evaluations.

The algorithm combines within-cell variation bounds, inherited cumulative confidence rectangles, and adaptive refinement in a useful way. The phase-by-phase description and illustrations make the main design understandable.

The experiments include 10 sampled functions with five runs each, give competitors larger evaluation budgets, and report computational costs alongside prediction quality. The substantial runtime difference between theoretical and reduced tree depths is informative.
weaknesses: Necessary: Important steps supporting Theorem 1 require correction. In Corollary 1, V_h is undefined at h=0 because it contains log(h²). Substituting the stated u into Lemma 7 also produces 2h log N, whereas V_h contains only h log N, so the displayed uniform-confidence argument does not establish the stated probability. In Lemma 14, equation (31) assumes that a previously refined parent still satisfies the refinement condition at the current evaluation count. This does not follow from decreasing posterior variance because β increases. A corrected analysis should use the confidence rectangle inherited at the actual refinement time or otherwise justify this inequality, then propagate the corrections through the sample-complexity bounds.

Necessary: Proposition 1 does not establish the claimed linear information gain under the stated assumptions. Its final lower bound contains a factor involving a_Tj²/(a_Tj²+σ²), which can vanish with T. Keeping the independent bump variances bounded below instead creates infinitely many points separated by a positive distance in the GP-induced metric, contradicting compactness together with Assumption 1. For the constructed sequence, vanishing variances give vanishing average information per observation. The assertion that a suitable metric resolves the issue is insufficient. Replace this example with a valid comparison or remove the corresponding separation claim.

Necessary: Definition 10 needs explicit handling of equal lower-bound vectors. Its weak-dominance condition can exclude every maximizer when multiple nodes have identical maximal lower bounds, leaving the pessimistic Pareto set empty. With two identical narrow upper boxes and a third narrow, substantially inferior box, no discarding occurs and the inferior node remains undecided even when every diameter is below ε. This undermines the maximal-witness argument in Lemma 3. Specify how representatives are retained and update the algorithm and proof consistently.

Necessary: The experimental metrics are inconsistent with the formal definitions. Section 7.1 describes accuracy by checking whether a predicted point is ε-dominated by a true Pareto point; an arbitrarily inferior prediction passes that test, although it lies outside Z_ε. The coverage description also switches between ε and 2ε as if they were equivalent. Table 2 averages accuracy and coverage into one number, preventing separate assessment of the two requirements. State the exact predicates, verify or recompute the results, and report both metrics separately. Explain how returned cells and baseline point sets are represented during evaluation, since output density affects coverage and MSE.

Necessary: Restrict the empirical conclusions to what was tested. The experiments cover one one-dimensional setting with two independent squared-exponential objectives; they do not establish broad superiority or demonstrate benefits from modeling dependent objectives. Setting V_h=0 at reduced depth removes the justified within-cell variation bound, so those faster variants do not inherit Theorem 1's guarantee. This distinction should be explicit. Likewise, a mean accuracy/coverage percentage does not directly validate the probability of returning an entirely ε-accurate set.

Optional: A controlled comparison with fixed discretization, correlated-output examples, additional input dimensions, and accuracy-versus-evaluation curves would help identify when adaptation is useful. These extensions are optional if the claims are appropriately restricted; the current recommendation rests on unresolved correctness and evidence concerns.
